content:
Getting to shops, appointments and social activities can become hard with arthritis and frailty, especially if you no longer drive.

This guide explains transport options that may help. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Community transport schemes

  • Dial-a-ride door-to-door minibuses.
  • Volunteer car schemes.
  • Shopping trips and group outings.
  • Community transport is usually run by charities and may charge a fare.

Bus passes

Older people and some disabled people can get free bus travel. Disabled people may be eligible for a disabled person's bus pass. Contact your council.

Hospital appointments

NHS non-emergency patient transport is available for people whose medical condition means they need it. Ask your GP or hospital. You may also be able to claim travel costs if you receive certain benefits.

Finding a scheme

Search the Community Transport Association website, or ask your council or local Age UK.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Is community transport free?

Some schemes are free, but many charge a fare.

Can a carer travel with me?

Many schemes allow this. Check when booking.

Sources and further reading

  • Community Transport Association
  • GOV.UK: Apply for a disabled person's bus pass
  • Age UK: Understanding frailty
